CHAPTER 10: A GUIDE TO THE CITIZENSHIP PROJECT REPORT (CPR)

OVERVIEW
- Active Citizenship strand. Learning Outcomes 3.1-3.6 and 4.1-4.5.
- The CPR assesses a student's ability 'to use the knowledge and concepts of Politics and Society to make judgements as to how to be active in communities' and their 'capacity to reflect upon and evaluate what they have learned or achieved from being an active participant in civil, social and political life'.
- Involves research, data analysis, effective action and extended reflection; draws on all key skills, especially working with others and being personally effective.
- Worth 100 marks = 20% of the grade at both Higher and Ordinary Level.
- Can be done individually or in groups (groups of no more than four recommended), but each report focuses on the candidate's OWN role, aims, actions, learning, development and reflection.
- Group pros: more actions, divided workload. Cons: need teamwork skills to work cohesively.

THE THREE SECTIONS
- Section A (35 marks): rationale for the action; summary of research, findings and sources (listed on a separate references/bibliography page).
- Section B (45 marks): summary of action taken; critical analysis of the action plan; outcomes.
- Section C (20 marks): critical reflection on knowledge gained and skills developed.
- The CPR has three aspects: research, action and reflection.

SIX-STEP CPR PROCESS
- 1. Brainstorm; 2. Proposal; 3. Feedback; 4. Research; 5. Implementation; 6. Review and type up.

STEP 1: BRAINSTORM
- Whole-class brainstorm: put four CPR titles on A3 paper in the four corners of the room.
- Go to the title that interests you most; with like-minded students, brainstorm avenues, questions, actions, issues and research; write on the A3 sheet.
- Rotate to your second choice and repeat for all titles; share back to the class - a 'treasure trove' of ideas.
- Choose the idea that inspires you most; see if you can form a group with others interested (discuss with teacher).

STEP 2: PROPOSAL
- Browse CPR titles in the brief from the SEC (State Examinations Commission).
- Tips for choosing a title: one that stands out; one you are interested in; one with an achievable action; one with links to parts of the course you enjoyed or want to learn more about.
- Proposal Part 1 (idea, rationale, research): which title and why; a research question narrowing the title (e.g. one aspect of gender inequality); link to course learning; aims; rationale; individual or group?
- Proposal Part 2 (execution): possible actions; brief action plan; hoped-for outcomes.
- Example titles/case studies: 2022 - rise of racism and anti-racism movements (Black Lives Matter popular); 2023 - causes and consequences of terrorism (fall of US-backed Afghan government and Taliban takeover); 2023 - does the status of women in Ireland reflect the status of democracy (Citizens' Assembly on Gender Equality, established 2020); 2024 - sportswashing as a political and human rights issue (Men's FIFA World Cup in Qatar 2022); 2024 - role of an NGO in a humanitarian crisis (NGOs helping those affected by Russia's invasion of Ukraine); 2022 - social media influencers' political power over young people (US voter registration soared when Taylor Swift encouraged followers on Instagram to vote).

STEP 3: FEEDBACK
- Meet your teacher regularly and log all feedback - you must reflect on it in the write-up.
- Argue your rationale to your teacher; agree an approach; implement feedback.
- Log and use feedback from organisations, colleagues, friends and anyone you interact with.

STEP 4: RESEARCH
- One of the most important parts; a large hub of research must inform your actions.
- Desk research: gathering and analysing existing data from books, journals, government reports and online databases (not collecting new data).
- Primary research: collecting new data directly from people through surveys, interviews, observations or experiments.
- Aim for at least three quantitative/qualitative pieces of data; may do own data analysis (survey, interviews); summarise findings; reference everything in the bibliography.
- Desk research pitfalls: relying on one source causes researcher bias - use reputable international organisations, news outlets, academic journals and books. Beware misinformation and fake news; check credibility and reliability.
- Confirmation bias: seeking or cherry-picking information that fits your existing beliefs. Keep an open mind; if you hold a political ideology, seek out contrasting viewpoints.
- Primary research pitfalls:
- Sampling bias: a sample that is not representative or lacks diversity gives skewed results (e.g. surveying only one age group or region on political attitudes).
- Question bias/wording: leading or loaded questions manipulate answers; use neutral language.
- Researcher bias: your tone, body language or cues may influence participants; stay neutral in collecting and analysing data.

STEP 5: IMPLEMENTATION
- Carry out informed action - actions must be informed by research. Research itself (survey, interview) is also an action.
- Each title has a specific action, e.g. 'plan and deliver an event that would raise awareness about this issue'.
- Be creative: whole-school initiatives (student council, board of management - awareness day, fundraiser, policy change); local community (Tidy Towns, local representatives, county council, community event); national (Dáil na nÓg, local TDs, joining a national movement).
- Critique actions as you go: what goes well/badly, how to adapt; find solutions, compromises or alternatives; summarise outcomes of each action; keep meeting your teacher and record how you acted on feedback.

STEP 6: REVIEW AND TYPE UP
- The CPR is a typed report in a Word booklet released by the SEC each year.
- Review prompts: what did you learn about the issue; new skills; what went well and what would you change; feedback and how you acted on it; links to the course.

THINGS TO REMEMBER
- Use headings: the 2019 Chief Examiner's Report recommended headings for strong structure; use the sub-headings from the Student Activity and Case Study Book and the SEC marking scheme.
- Appendix (images, charts, tables) is optional - no marks; never include material that identifies you, others or your school (e.g. photos).
- Word count: stick to it, especially in Section A Summary and Sources. Show 'skilful brevity' - key findings only.
- Plagiarism: copying, improper help or work by others is investigated by the SEC. Penalties (Rules and Programme for Secondary Schools): loss of coursework marks, loss of the subject, loss of the whole exam in all subjects, or being barred from future Certificate Exams. Giving inappropriate help is an offence under the Education Act 1998.

SUCCESS CRITERIA - SECTION A: RATIONALE AND RESEARCH (35 marks incl. bibliography)
- Explanation for Rationale (7): why you are doing it, justification, what inspired you - a current event or course topic. Must link to the course and give a specific case study. Sample: LGBTQ+-inclusive education, inspired by Topic 5 human rights and David Norris's ECHR case to decriminalise homosexuality in Ireland.
- Aims (4): what you aim to achieve; clearly identifiable; at least three aims. Sample: why teenage girls drop out of sport - highlight dropout rates, encourage support for women's sport, deepen own understanding.
- Action Plan and Means (8): your plan and how (means) you will achieve the aims. Sample: desk research on dropout rates; school and community survey via school platforms and social media; compare with general data to check for geographic/socio-economic bias; report to local news outlet and councillor.
- Summary and Sources (12): concise summary of findings from many sources and own primary research; use shorthand references (1), (2), (3) linked to the bibliography. Sample: human trafficking of refugees - industry profit $150 billion a year; second largest criminal industry after drugs; Ireland one of two weakest EU states with Romania, Tier 2 'watchlist', no convictions since 2013 amendment; 2.5 million victims a year, 40-50% children, 80% women; about 90% of over 3.6 million Ukrainian refugees are women and children; own survey of 1,250 people - only 25% aware, 90% wanted more information.
- Bibliography and References (4): recommended full Harvard style - Author (Year) Title. Where published: Publisher. E.g. Reilly, J. (2006) Using Statistics. Dublin: Gill and Macmillan. Websites need the web address and date accessed. Original research can be listed (e.g. 'Original Research. (2022) A Quantitative Survey of Irish Travellers').

SECTION B: EXECUTION OF CPR (45 marks)
- Summary of the Actions Taken (15): use 'we'/'I'; briefly list all main actions; do NOT comment on how they went. Should include research actions and actions acting on research; refer back to the action in the title. Sample: survey on ableism shared on social media and in school; graphics of results; emails to AsIAm and Down Syndrome Ireland for videos shared on Microsoft Teams; letter to the Minister for Disability.
- Critical Analysis of CPR Action Plan (15): what went well and what did not; refer back to the plan; at least three examples, mix of positive and negative; show how you overcame adversity (no one expects a perfect CPR). Sample: Covid-19 cancelled a Sustainable Clothes Swap, so they pivoted to a workshop with pamphlets (contingency plan); survey showed younger years knew least, so they were targeted; quiz software problems solved with teacher help; unreliable Wi-Fi solved using a personal hotspot.
- Summary of Outcomes (15): what you achieved; refer back to aims; did actions have impact; wider community? Sample on greenwashing: entry and exit surveys - 80% did not know what greenwashing was; 90% afterwards wanted to act; poster competition; resources shared with Geography, Science, Business and Politics departments; article on interview with MEP Grace O'Sullivan in newsletter and social media.

SECTION C: REFLECTIONS ON KNOWLEDGE AND SKILLS (20 marks)
- Knowledge and Insights Gained about the Issue (6): what you learned about the TOPIC, not the process; be specific; link to course concepts. Sample: smartphone age restriction - digital literacy improves safety and misinformation recognition; denying smartphones could infringe freedom of expression, association and access to information; parents as primary educators.
- Skills (6): explain at least three skills and how you developed them (research, data collection, teamwork, graphic design, public speaking). Sample (Iranian regime after death of Mahsa Amini): desk and primary research, quantitative survey, extracting key data, public speaking in a workshop.
- Reflection (4): what went well overall and one thing you would do differently. Sample: would contact NGOs such as Amnesty International for feedback.
- Feedback and Learning from the Course (4): feedback received and how you ACTED on it; course learning used. Sample (votes for Irish emigrants): teacher suggested networks of Irish abroad, e.g. Enterprise Ireland; respondent suggested a 'prefer not to say' option; linked to Kwame Anthony Appiah's cosmopolitanism, internationalism and globalisation.

rows.prompt: What percentage of the Politics and Society grade is the CPR worth?
rows.explanation: The CPR is 100 marks, or 20% of the grade at both Higher and Ordinary Level.

rows.prompt: How many marks is the CPR worth in total?
rows.explanation: The report is marked out of 100.

rows.prompt: How many marks is Section B (Execution of CPR) worth?
rows.explanation: Section A is 35, Section B is 45 and Section C is 20 marks.

rows.prompt: What does Section C of the CPR focus on?
rows.explanation: Section C (20 marks) asks for critical reflection on knowledge gained and skills developed.

rows.prompt: If you do the CPR in a group, what must your report focus on?
options: Your own individual role, actions and learning
rows.explanation: Each report focuses on the candidate's own role, aims, actions, learning and reflection.

rows.prompt: What is the recommended maximum group size for a CPR?
rows.explanation: It is not recommended to have a group larger than four people.

rows.prompt: What is the first step of the six-step CPR process?
rows.explanation: The steps are brainstorm, proposal, feedback, research, implementation, review and type up.

rows.prompt: Which step comes straight after the proposal?
rows.explanation: After the proposal you meet your teacher for feedback.

rows.prompt: Which body releases the CPR titles and booklet each year?
rows.explanation: The SEC releases the brief and a new Word booklet each year.

rows.prompt: Which is a tip for choosing a CPR title?
options: Choose one with an achievable action
Choose the one with the fewest links to the course
Choose the one needing no research
rows.explanation: Tips: one that stands out, interests you, has an achievable action and links to the course.

rows.prompt: Gathering existing data from books, journals and government reports is called:
rows.explanation: Desk research uses existing data rather than new surveys or interviews.

rows.prompt: Collecting new data through surveys or interviews is called:
rows.explanation: Primary research collects new data directly from people.

rows.prompt: Cherry-picking information that fits your existing beliefs is called:
rows.explanation: Confirmation bias means seeking information that aligns with your opinions.

rows.prompt: Surveying only one age group about political attitudes risks:
rows.explanation: A sample that is not representative gives skewed results that cannot be generalised.

rows.prompt: Asking leading or loaded questions in a survey causes:
rows.explanation: The wording of questions can manipulate answers, so use neutral language.

rows.prompt: Influencing participants through your tone or body language is an example of:
rows.explanation: Researcher bias comes from the researcher's own cues; you should stay neutral.

rows.prompt: At least how many pieces of quantitative/qualitative data should you aim to find?
rows.explanation: The chapter says try to find at least three pieces of data.

rows.prompt: Which is true about actions in the CPR?
options: Research does not count as an action
Actions should be decided before research
Actions must be informed by research
rows.explanation: Actions need to be informed by research, and research such as a survey is itself an action.

rows.prompt: Which national youth body is suggested for a CPR action with national impact?
rows.explanation: Students could link with national organisations such as Dáil na nÓg or local TDs.

rows.prompt: What did the 2019 Chief Examiner's Report recommend for the type-up?
options: Using headings to create a strong structure
rows.explanation: Headings help structure the report and maximise marks.

rows.prompt: How many marks does the optional appendix earn?
rows.explanation: Students receive no marks for material in the appendix.

rows.prompt: Under which Act is giving a student inappropriate CPR help an offence?
rows.explanation: Providing inappropriate assistance is an offence under the Education Act 1998.

rows.prompt: Which is a possible penalty for plagiarism in the CPR?
options: Loss of the entire examination in all subjects
rows.explanation: Penalties range from losing coursework marks to losing all subjects or being barred in later years.

rows.prompt: How many marks is the Explanation for Rationale worth?
rows.explanation: Rationale 7, Aims 4, Action Plan and Means 8, Summary and Sources 12, Bibliography 4.

rows.prompt: How many aims should a CPR have, at least?
rows.explanation: You should have at least three clearly identifiable aims.

rows.prompt: Which part of Section A carries the most marks?
rows.explanation: Summary and Sources is worth 12 marks.

rows.prompt: Which referencing style is recommended for the bibliography?
rows.explanation: Harvard: Author (Year) Title. Where published: Publisher; websites need the address and date accessed.

rows.prompt: In the Summary of the Actions Taken, you should:
options: briefly list actions without commenting on how they went
list only the actions that went well
rows.explanation: Critique belongs in the Critical Analysis; the summary just lists actions.

rows.prompt: In the Critical Analysis of the Action Plan, you should include:
options: at least three examples, both positive and negative
rows.explanation: Include a mix of positive and negative examples and show how you overcame problems.

rows.prompt: 'Knowledge and Insights Gained' should be about:
options: what you learned about the CPR process
what you learned about the issue itself
rows.explanation: This section is about your specific topic, not the process.

rows.prompt: Since the Skills section is worth six marks, you should explain at least:
rows.explanation: The chapter says explain at least three skills and how you developed them.

rows.prompt: Name the three sections of the CPR and their marks.
rows.model_answer: Section A, Rationale and Research, is worth 35 marks including the bibliography. Section B, Execution of the CPR, is worth 45 marks. Section C, Reflections on Knowledge and Skills, is worth 20 marks, making 100 marks or 20% of the grade.

rows.prompt: List the six steps of the CPR process.
rows.model_answer: 1. Brainstorm, 2. Proposal, 3. Feedback, 4. Research, 5. Implementation, and 6. Review and type up. Feedback from the teacher should be logged throughout.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between desk research and primary research, with an example of each.
rows.model_answer: Desk research gathers and analyses existing data from books, journals, government reports and online databases, such as CSO census figures. Primary research collects new data directly from people through surveys, interviews, observations or experiments, such as a survey of your school.

rows.prompt: Describe three types of bias to avoid when doing CPR research.
rows.model_answer: Confirmation bias is cherry-picking information that fits your existing beliefs. Sampling bias happens when your sample is not representative, such as surveying only one age group. Question bias comes from leading or loaded questions; researcher bias comes from your tone or body language influencing participants.

rows.prompt: Give examples of CPR actions at school, local and national level.
rows.model_answer: At school: an awareness day or fundraiser with the student council or board of management. Locally: a community event with Tidy Towns, local representatives or the county council. Nationally: linking with Dáil na nÓg or local TDs, or joining a national movement.

rows.prompt: What should a strong Explanation for Rationale include?
rows.model_answer: It should explain directly why you are doing the project and what inspired you, such as a current event or course topic. It must link the CPR to the Politics and Society course and mention a specific case study or example, such as David Norris's case at the ECHR in the sample on LGBTQ+-inclusive education.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between the Summary of Actions and the Critical Analysis in Section B.
rows.model_answer: The Summary of Actions briefly lists everything you did using 'I' or 'we', without commenting on how it went. The Critical Analysis evaluates the actions against your plan, giving at least three examples of what went well and badly and how you adapted, such as switching a cancelled clothes swap to a workshop.

rows.prompt: State three things to remember when typing up the CPR.
rows.model_answer: Use headings from the Student Activity and Case Study Book and marking scheme, as the 2019 Chief Examiner's Report recommended. Keep to the word count and show 'skilful brevity', especially in Summary and Sources. Do not plagiarise, and do not include material in the appendix that identifies you or your school.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between quantitative and qualitative research, and give one example of each that could be used in a Citizenship Project Report. (5 marks)
rows.model_answer: Quantitative research gives numerical data, such as a survey of 1,250 people showing that only 25% were aware of human trafficking of refugees. Qualitative research gives in-depth views and experiences in words, such as an interview or focus group with members of an organisation.
rows.marking_scheme: Difference explained: 2 marks. Quantitative example: 1.5 marks. Qualitative example: 1.5 marks. Accept surveys/statistics/CSO data for quantitative; interviews/focus groups/written responses for qualitative.

rows.prompt:
A student surveyed 30 classmates in their own Politics and Society class on the question: 'Don't you agree that the voting age should be lowered to 16?' 90% answered yes. The student concluded that most young people in Ireland want the voting age lowered.

Evaluate the quality of this research and the conclusion drawn. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: The research is weak and the conclusion is not justified. First, there is sampling bias: 30 students from one Politics and Society class is a small sample and not representative of all young people in Ireland, since they share an age, school and interest in politics. Second, there is question bias: 'Don't you agree...' is a leading question that pushes people to say yes. Third, there may be researcher bias, as classmates may give the answer they think the student wants. Because of this, the 90% figure cannot be generalised. A better study would use a larger, more diverse sample from different schools and regions, and a neutral question such as 'Should the voting age be lowered to 16? Yes / No / Unsure'.
rows.marking_scheme: 4 points x 2.5 marks: sampling bias (small/unrepresentative sample); question bias (leading wording); researcher bias or peer pressure; conclusion cannot be generalised; suggested improvement (larger diverse sample, neutral wording, desk research from several sources to avoid confirmation bias).

rows.prompt: Describe two ways a student could take informed action on an issue affecting their community, and explain why research is important before acting. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: One way is a whole-school initiative, such as an awareness day or fundraiser run with the student council or board of management, or using school power structures to push for policy change. A second way is a community or national action, such as writing to a TD or minister, linking with a local councillor or Tidy Towns, or joining a national movement through Dáil na nÓg. Research is important because actions must be informed by evidence. Desk research and surveys show what people know and need; for example, one CPR survey showed younger students knew least about fast fashion, so the workshop targeted them. Research also gives credible facts to share and prevents spreading misinformation.
rows.marking_scheme: 2 actions x 3 marks (1 statement + 2 explanation). Importance of research: 4 marks (2 points x 2), e.g. actions must be informed, identifies target audience/needs, gives credible evidence, avoids misinformation/bias.

rows.prompt: 'Taking part in active citizenship is as important as learning about politics in the classroom.' Discuss, with reference to the process of carrying out a Citizenship Project Report. (40 marks)
rows.model_answer:
I agree that active citizenship is as important as classroom learning, because the two strengthen each other. The CPR is designed to test a student's ability 'to use the knowledge and concepts of Politics and Society to make judgements as to how to be active in communities' and to reflect on being 'an active participant in civil, social and political life'.

First, active citizenship turns knowledge into action. Students must take informed action, such as an awareness day with the student council, contacting a TD or minister, or linking with Dáil na nÓg. In one sample, students surveyed people on ableism, got videos from AsIAm and Down Syndrome Ireland for their school and wrote to the Minister for Disability.

Second, it builds real skills. Students carry out desk and primary research and learn to avoid confirmation, sampling, question and researcher bias. They develop teamwork, public speaking and data-handling skills, and learn to adapt; in one CPR, when Covid-19 cancelled a clothes swap, the group changed to a workshop with pamphlets.

Third, it can create change. The greenwashing sample showed 80% of students did not know what greenwashing was before the workshop, and 90% wanted to act afterwards.

However, classroom learning remains essential. Rationales must link to the course, such as Topic 5 on human rights, and reflections draw on thinkers like Kwame Anthony Appiah's cosmopolitanism. Without this knowledge, action can be poorly informed. Active projects also face limits: small surveys may not be representative, and one student's action may have limited reach.

Overall, active citizenship is as important as classroom learning, because it lets students apply, test and reflect on what they learn.
rows.marking_scheme: Marked for: clear position stated and sustained (8 marks); understanding of the aims and structure of the CPR / active citizenship (8 marks); examples and evidence from the chapter, e.g. sample actions, survey results, research methods and biases, skills (14 marks); counter-argument, e.g. need for course knowledge, limits of small-scale action (6 marks); conclusion (4 marks).
